name: Legend
vendor: FINOS (Linux Foundation), started at Goldman Sachs

foundation.via: Incubating since its open-source release on October 19, 2020

summary: Goldman Sachs’s data modelling and governance platform, open-sourced through FINOS: describe business concepts once in the Pure language, map them to databases and services, and query or publish them as APIs while the engine generates the SQL.
intro: Legend puts a shared model between data and the people who use it. In Legend Studio, a web-based modelling environment with a visual editor and a text grammar, you define classes such as `Trade` or `Person`, with typed properties, multiplicities, associations and constraints that act as data-quality rules. Mappings connect each class to where the data really lives: tables in a relational store, other models, or service and document stores. Legend Engine, a Java server, takes a query written against the model, such as all trades filtered by desk and projected to a few columns, builds an execution plan and generates SQL for the database behind it. The engine ships extensions for about 20 relational databases, including Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, Athena, Trino, Presto, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, DuckDB, Spanner, Oracle, SQL Server and DB2. Lineage from source to query is computed from the mappings.

Around the model sit the other pieces. Legend SDLC stores models as entities in GitLab projects, so changes go through branches, reviews and versioned releases, and Legend Depot serves a read-only REST API over the published versions, which it loads from a Maven-style repository. Legend Query gives non-engineers a drag-and-drop query builder; any query can be promoted to a Legend Service, a REST endpoint backed by the same SDLC; and `pylegend` is a Python client. Models can also be translated to JSON Schema, Protobuf and Avro. Goldman Sachs built the platform internally as Alloy, with Pure as its language, and released five modules through FINOS in October 2020. FINOS runs a free shared instance for open, industry modelling work such as its Financial Objects special interest group, whose models are all public.
strengths: One model of business concepts, with constraints and lineage, mapped to many databases, so queries are written against names like `Trade.desk` and compiled to each store’s SQL
Models are managed like code: versioned in GitLab through Legend SDLC, reviewed, released as artifacts and served to other tools by Legend Depot
The same query can be run ad hoc in Legend Query, published as a REST service or called from Python, and models can generate JSON Schema, Protobuf and Avro
Used across Goldman Sachs’s divisions for years before its release, and Apache 2.0 licensed under FINOS
limits: A heavy deployment: Studio, Engine, SDLC and Depot are separate services, and production needs GitLab with OAuth, SSL certificates and an identity provider; Docker Compose is meant only for a proof of concept
Pure is a language of its own, with its own grammar for models, mappings and queries, and few people outside the banks that use Legend know it
Still incubating at FINOS six years after its release, the stage for projects in their early growth phase
The FINOS shared instance is only for open models: every project in it maps to a public GitLab project, so proprietary models need your own installation

story: Goldman Sachs developed the platform for about seven years before releasing it, under the internal names Alloy for the platform and PURE for its language, as a way to keep data consistent across the many applications that use the same business concepts. Engineers and non-engineers across all of the bank’s divisions used it.

FINOS accepted the contribution in January 2020. From April to September 2020 a pilot ran a shared Legend instance on FINOS infrastructure, where Deutsche Bank, Morgan Stanley, RBC Capital Markets and others worked on extensions to ISDA’s Common Domain Model and on commodities reference data. On October 19, 2020 Goldman Sachs open-sourced five modules, Legend Studio, Legend Engine, Legend SDLC, Legend Shared and the Legend Pure language, under the new name Legend, chosen to present one platform for its data strategy.

The shared instance stayed open for industry modelling, and FINOS’s Financial Objects special interest group uses it for open financial data standards. Later additions included Legend Depot, Legend Query, a Python client and engine extensions for cloud warehouses. In October 2026 the FINOS landscape still listed Legend as incubating.

choices.why: Business concepts such as a trade are defined once and mapped to wherever the data lives, so consumers query names that mean the same thing in every application instead of each team’s tables.

choices.choice: Models in GitLab, not a metadata database
choices.why: Treating models as versioned code gives them reviews, releases and dependencies, so a change to a shared definition is controlled like a change to a library.

choices.choice: A visual editor on top of a text language
choices.why: Goldman wanted one platform for engineers and non-engineers: Studio lets analysts build models visually while the same model is stored as Pure text that engineers can diff and review.
